analysis.one_liner: Cuts student loan interest rates, raises Pell Grants, caps loan payments to income, and ends lender subsidies.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 273-149 and the Senate 78-18, cleared a conference committee with large bipartisan votes (Senate 79-12, House 292-97), and was signed into law as Public Law 110-84 in September 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The law raises the maximum Pell Grant for low-income college students in steps through 2012-2013, cuts the interest rate on need-based undergraduate student loans from 6.8% to 3.4%, and creates income-based repayment that caps monthly payments at 15% of income above the poverty line, canceling anything still owed after 25 years. It forgives Direct Loans for borrowers who work 10 years in public service jobs, and creates TEACH Grants of $4,000 a year for students who commit to teaching high-need subjects in high-need schools. The cost is offset by cutting federal subsidies, fees, and default-insurance payments to private student lenders and guaranty agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income college students get larger Pell Grants and more generous need calculations, including new protections for foster youth, homeless youth, and children of dislocated workers. Undergraduate borrowers get interest rates phased down to 3.4%. Struggling borrowers get income-based repayment with forgiveness after 25 years, and public-service workers (teachers, nurses, government and nonprofit employees) get loan cancellation after 120 payments. Prospective teachers in high-need fields get up to $16,000 in TEACH Grants. Minority-serving colleges and Upward Bound programs receive new funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income college students and student borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum Pell Grant by $490, then $690, then $1,090 over the 2008-09 through 2012-13 award years, paid from mandatory appropriations [S6][S7][S8].
Phases the interest rate on need-based undergraduate loans down from 6.8% to 3.4% by July 2011 [S7][S8].

Creates income-based repayment capping monthly payments at 15% of income above 150% of the poverty line, with any remaining balance canceled after 25 years, and forgives Direct Loans entirely after 120 payments by borrowers in public service jobs [S7][S8].

Provides up to $1,000 per year in loan forgiveness for early childhood educators, nurses, librarians, child welfare workers, and other national-need service, and $4,000-per-year TEACH Grants for future teachers [S6][S8].

Expands Pell eligibility by raising income protection allowances for working students, raising the automatic-zero family-contribution income limit from $20,000 to $30,000, and treating foster youth and verified homeless youth as independent students [S7].
Provides $255 million a year to Hispanic-serving, historically Black, tribal, and other minority-serving institutions, and $57 million a year to restore cut Upward Bound projects [S6][S7].

analysis.who_pays: Private FFEL student lenders and guaranty agencies lose billions in federal subsidies: special allowance payments are cut, the lender loan fee doubles to 1%, guaranty agencies' share of defaulted-loan collections falls from 23% to 16%, their account maintenance fee drops from 0.10% to 0.06%, 'exceptional performer' bonuses end, and federal default insurance falls to 95%. The bill's new spending is funded through the budget reconciliation process using those savings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student lenders and guaranty agencies

drawbacks.text: TEACH Grants convert to a loan with interest from the date of each award if the recipient does not complete four years of teaching in a high-need school, a penalty that has caught many recipients [S8].
Public-service loan forgiveness applies only to Direct Loans, so FFEL borrowers must consolidate into the Direct Loan program to qualify [S8].
Income-based repayment stretches repayment out to as long as 25 years before forgiveness, and unpaid interest can be capitalized when a borrower leaves the plan [S7][S8].

The tuition-pressure provisions the House passed — bonus grants for colleges that hold tuition increases to the Higher Education Price Index — were dropped in conference, and the final law only requires high-cost colleges to file reports explaining price increases, without any penalty [S4] vs. [S6][S7].
The Pell increases were smaller in the final law than the House version's, which would have raised the authorized maximum to $11,600 by 2012-13 [S3][S4] vs. [S6][S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to students and borrowers are large and concrete: bigger grants, cheaper loans, a realistic escape hatch from unaffordable payments, and forgiveness for public-service work. The costs fall mainly on private lenders and guaranty agencies that were receiving above-market federal subsidies, plus new federal spending covered by those cuts. The main design flaws are the TEACH Grant's convert-to-loan penalty and the weakness of the final tuition-restraint provisions, which the conference committee stripped to reporting requirements.

outcome.mechanism: It passed both chambers, survived a conference committee, and was signed by President Bush on September 27, 2007, becoming Public Law 110-84 [S7][S10].

narrative.text: Introduced June 12, 2007 by Rep. George Miller, the House Education and Labor Committee reported it 30-16 on June 25 [S10].
The House passed it 273-149 on July 11, with Democrats voting 226-0 and Republicans 47-149 [S12].
In the Senate, the motion to proceed passed 49-48 along party lines, with all 48 voting Republicans opposed [S13].
The Senate passed the bill 78-18 on July 20, with 29 Republicans joining all Democrats [S14].

A House Republican motion to recommit — which would have barred elected officials and registered lobbyists from the bill's loan forgiveness programs — failed 199-223, with 195 of 201 House Republicans in favor [S11].
The conference report passed the Senate 79-12 and the House 292-97 on September 7, with 34 Senate Republicans and 77 House Republicans voting yes [S16][S17].
President Bush signed it on September 27, 2007 as Public Law 110-84 [S7][S10].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income students, borrowers, and public-service workers gained larger grants and cheaper, more forgiving loans; private student lenders and guaranty agencies lost federal subsidies they had been receiving.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Students and borrowers, at lenders' expense

sides.party_line_note: The House passed it 226-0 among Democrats against 47-149 among Republicans, and the Senate's first procedural vote was 47-48 on party lines, but the final conference votes were bipartisan, with 77 House Republicans and 34 Senate Republicans joining every Democrat.

industries.note: The bill cuts the federal special allowance payments that compensate lenders for the gap between fixed loan rates and market rates, doubles the lender loan fee to 1%, and cuts default insurance from 97% to 95%. These subsidized payments were the industry's profit engine, and cutting them paid for the student aid increases.

Guaranty agencies' share of collections on defaulted federal loans drops from 23% to 16%, their account maintenance fee falls from 0.10% to 0.06%, and the 'exceptional performer' bonus program is eliminated.

industries.industry: Nonprofit and state student loan holders
industries.note: The law creates a protected 'eligible not-for-profit holder' category with somewhat higher federal subsidy rates than for-profit lenders receive, and requires in-state nonprofit lenders to have existed at enactment to qualify. This locks nonprofit and state entities into the loan program as favored intermediaries.

Federal Pell, TEACH, and minority-institution funds flow through colleges, deepening their role as the channel for federal student aid. The law also requires schools whose prices rise much faster than the Higher Education Price Index to report explanations, but the House's bonus grants for holding tuition down were dropped in conference, leaving the pressure largely reputational.
